title: The comma operator
recap: The built-in comma operator evaluates its left operand, discards that result, then evaluates and yields its right operand. Its sequencing can be useful in narrow contexts, but separate statements are usually clearer.

The comma operator has very low precedence, so parentheses are normally required when its yielded value is assigned. Commas also separate function arguments and declarations; those commas are separators, not comma operators.
objectives: Use the built-in comma operator in an explicitly parenthesized expression.
Observe a side effect from the left operand before evaluating the right operand.
Distinguish the comma operator from punctuation that separates declarations.
Prefer clear sequencing outside the focused demonstration.
warnings: Without parentheses, assignment binds more tightly than the comma operator.
Do not treat every comma token in C++ as the comma operator.
Avoid hiding multiple complicated side effects in a comma expression.
challenge: Start auditCode at 4. In one clearly parenthesized comma expression, add 2 to auditCode in the left operand and calculate auditCode * 3 in the right operand. Store the yielded right-hand value in auditResult and print the final code and result.
hints: The left operand can be auditCode += 2, which both mutates auditCode and yields a value that the comma operator discards.
Use auditCode * 3 as the right operand; that is the value the full comma expression yields.
The initializer needs double parentheses around the comma expression: int auditResult{ (left, right) };.
